title: The Peterman Pod × Ethan Evans — 礼貌的虚构
title_en: The Peterman Pod × Ethan Evans — The Polite Fiction

questions.question: 按 Ethan Evans 讲的「礼貌的虚构」（polite fiction），想争取更大的地盘时，哪种说法最符合这套做法？
options: 「我对扩大地盘没兴趣」——先隐藏意图，等机会自己送上门
「把他的组划给我，不然我就考虑另一个部门给的 offer」——把筹码直接摆上桌
「如果重组需要人顶上，我在，而且不打算走」——诉求不变，只换成无私的样子
「他的组管得不好，大家都看在眼里」——先削弱对手，再提出接手
questions.explanation: 礼貌的虚构不是撒谎，也不是藏起诉求：底意仍是「有什么我都接」，只是说成像无私的仆人，两者可以同时为真。直接摆出「不给就走」是它刻意避开的海盗式说法。
questions.question_en: Under what Ethan Evans calls a "polite fiction," which line best fits how you should ask for a bigger scope?
options_en: "I have no interest in growing my scope" — hide the intent and wait for the opportunity to come
"Give me his team, or I'll take the other department's offer" — put your leverage right on the table
"If the reorg needs someone to step up, I'm here and not planning to leave" — same ask, framed as service
"Everyone can see his team is struggling" — weaken the rival first, then offer to take over
questions.explanation_en: A polite fiction is neither a lie nor a concealed ask: the underlying message is still "I'll take whatever comes," just delivered like a selfless servant, and both can be true at once. Stating "give it to me or I walk" is exactly the pirate version it avoids.

questions.question: Ethan Evans 建议想越级投诉直属经理时「别单独去」。他给的理由是什么？
options: 越级领导信你就多出三个麻烦，不信你则毫无麻烦，单人报告天然吃亏
单独去会被视为个人恩怨，几个人去能显得问题更有普遍性、更占道德高地
公司制度规定越级投诉至少需要两人联署，否则 HR 不会受理
几个人一起去，越级领导会觉得被挑战，反而更愿意保护提出问题的人
questions.explanation: 他站在越级领导的位置算账：相信一个人的投诉会带来三个麻烦，不信则没有麻烦，所以单个人的说法天然吃亏，几个人的说法先后传上来才会被认真对待。这不是制度要求，而是激励问题。
questions.question_en: Ethan Evans advises against going over your manager's head alone. What reasoning does he give?
options_en: If the skip-level believes you they inherit three problems, if not they have none, so a lone report starts behind
Going alone looks like a personal grudge, while a group looks principled and holds the moral high ground
Company policy requires at least two signatories before HR will accept a skip-level complaint
A group makes the skip-level feel challenged, which makes them more inclined to protect the people raising it
questions.explanation_en: He reasons from the skip-level's incentives: believing one complaint creates three problems, disbelieving creates none, so a lone report starts at a disadvantage. Only when several accounts arrive does it get taken seriously. It's an incentive problem, not a policy rule.

questions.question: Ethan Evans 区分了好的和坏的「背后沟通」（backchanneling）。下面哪种属于他说的好的那种，以及它为什么管用？
options: 会前单独问 CFO「我的方案你哪里不放心」，对方被咨询过就更愿支持你
会后再单独找决策者补充论据，因为会上的第一印象往往不是最终决定，还能翻盘
私下把会上不便公开说的顾虑告诉决策者，让对手的方案在会前就失分
会前先把方案的全部细节发给所有与会者，避免会上被临时提问难住
questions.explanation: 好的背后沟通是会前私下请教决策者的顾虑；它起作用不只因为交换了信息，更因为对方觉得被咨询过。拨款的人在算「出事时谁靠得住」，两个方案差不多时会给先来问过他的人。私下说公开场合不敢说的话，正是他说的坏的那种。
questions.question_en: Ethan Evans separates good backchanneling from bad. Which is the good kind, and why does it work?
options_en: Privately asking the CFO beforehand what worries them about your plan; having been consulted, they lean your way
Following up with the decision-maker after the meeting, since first impressions in the room are rarely final and can be reversed
Privately telling the decision-maker the concerns you can't voice in the meeting, so the rival plan loses ground early
Sending every attendee the full details ahead of time so you aren't caught off guard by questions
questions.explanation_en: Good backchanneling means privately asking the decision-maker about their concerns beforehand. It works not only through information exchange but because they feel consulted; a funder weighing "who can I count on" will back whoever came to them first when plans are close. Saying privately what you won't say publicly is his example of the bad kind.
